Overview

Prague as a Business Centre

Prague is the Czech Republic's capital and largest city, with 1,397,880 inhabitants on 31 December 2024 according to preliminary Czech Statistical Office data, after growth of more than 13,000 in that year driven mainly by migration. The city concentrates national government, the Czech National Bank, the Prague Stock Exchange and the head offices of most major banks, insurers, energy and industrial groups and their investment vehicles. Its economy is weighted toward financial and professional services, information technology, shared service centres, real estate, tourism and public administration. Prague is also a regional base for multinational companies covering Central and Eastern Europe, with business conducted in Czech and widely in English.

Organisations commission investigative work connected to Prague because Czech capital, and the people who control it, are often managed from the city even where assets lie elsewhere in Europe. Large privately held groups built since the 1990s hold energy, media, retail, real estate and financial assets across the continent through layered Czech, Dutch, Cypriot and Luxembourg structures. Investors, lenders and counterparties need to know who stands behind them. Public procurement and EU-funded projects decided in the capital carry integrity risk. Disputes frequently land in Prague, either before the courts or in its permanent arbitration institutions, and the research supporting them must work in Czech-language records.

Typical Matters

Investigative Work Connected to Prague

01

Ownership of Czech holding groups

Prague-based business groups often control assets through chains of Czech and foreign companies and trusts. We map these structures from commercial register filings, annual reports and foreign registries, identifying ultimate controllers, related parties and changes over time for investors, lenders and acquirers.

02

Procurement and EU funds integrity

Ministries and agencies based in Prague award contracts and administer EU-funded programmes. Bidders, partners and lenders face risk from undisclosed beneficial owners and conflicts of interest. We research ownership, political connections and prior enforcement of suppliers and subcontractors to support compliance decisions.

03

Real estate investment due diligence

Prague's office, residential and hospitality real estate attracts foreign capital. We review cadastral records, owning company histories, financing and litigation, and the backgrounds of sellers and developers, so that buyers understand title, encumbrances and the people they are dealing with before committing funds.

04

Arbitration and litigation support

Disputes seated in Prague arbitral institutions or heard by Prague courts often turn on facts about corporate control, asset transfers and witness histories. We work with counsel to gather and document public-record evidence in Czech and other relevant jurisdictions, consistent with procedural orders.

05

Regional hub counterparty screening

Many multinationals run Central and Eastern European operations from Prague, engaging distributors and agents across the region. We screen these counterparties for ownership, sanctions exposure, political exposure and adverse media in Czech and neighbouring languages before onboarding or renewal.

Local Context

Courts, Records and Institutions in Prague

Prague courts

Commercial disputes of higher value and corporate matters are generally heard at first instance by the regional courts; in the capital this role is performed by the Municipal Court in Prague, which also sits as the registry court for companies seated in Prague. Proceedings are conducted in Czech, and foreign documents require certified translation. First-instance cases commonly take 12 to 24 months, with appeals adding further time, so counsel often weighs arbitration or settlement alongside litigation.

Arbitration Court in Prague

The Arbitration Court attached to the Economic Chamber and Agricultural Chamber of the Czech Republic is based in Prague, with permanent hearing venues in Brno, Plzen, Ostrava and Hradec Kralove. Its rules, in a consolidated text dated 1 October 2015, leave much of the procedure to the tribunal; there is no emergency arbitrator, and interim measures are ordered only by the ordinary courts. Cases are generally resolved in under a year.

Prague Stock Exchange Arbitration Court

The Prague Stock Exchange operates a permanent arbitration court established under the Arbitration Act (Act No. 216/1994 Coll.) and the Capital Market Business Act (Act No. 254/2004 Coll.), based on the exchange's Czech National Bank licence to operate a regulated market. It hears disputes where the parties have agreed to its jurisdiction. Its arbitrators are listed by the exchange and are based in Prague.

Czech National Bank

The Czech National Bank, headquartered in Prague, is both the central bank and the integrated supervisor of the Czech financial market, including banks, insurers, investment firms and the stock exchange. Its licensing and sanctions decisions are a source when assessing regulated counterparties. Matters involving Prague-based financial institutions, funds or listed issuers usually require review of regulatory history alongside commercial register and court records.

Local investigative limits

Czech national rules on private detective services and data protection, described on the Czech Republic page, apply fully in Prague. In practice, any surveillance, interviews or attendance in the city is carried out by professionals holding the required Czech trade concession, and personal data is handled under the GDPR. TDSC does not hold a Czech concession and coordinates qualified local professionals for such work.

Engagement Standard

How TDSC Scopes Matters in Prague

TDSC has no office in Prague and handles Prague matters from Nashville. We begin with the purpose of the work, whether a transaction, a financing, a dispute before the Municipal Court or a Prague arbitral institution, or an internal review, and agree scope with the client's Czech counsel. Research uses the Czech commercial register and its collection of deeds, the cadastre, court decisions, Czech National Bank records and Czech-language media, and extends to the Dutch, Cypriot, Luxembourg or other registries where Prague groups hold assets. Fieldwork is carried out by Czech professionals holding the required concession. Personal data is processed under the GDPR with a documented purpose, and reports cite sources for use by counsel.

TDSC has no office in Prague. Engagements are directed from Nashville, Tennessee; where work on the ground is needed, it is performed by appropriately licensed local professionals under a written scope.

Questions

Prague: Frequently Asked Questions

Which court in Prague handles company disputes?

The Municipal Court in Prague acts as the regional court for the capital and hears higher-value commercial and corporate matters at first instance. It also serves as the registry court for companies seated in Prague. Proceedings are in Czech. We work with the client's Czech counsel to align research and translated evidence with the court's procedure.

Is Prague a practical place to arbitrate?

Prague hosts the Arbitration Court attached to the Economic Chamber and Agricultural Chamber of the Czech Republic and the Prague Stock Exchange Arbitration Court. Proceedings at the former are generally completed within a year. Interim measures must be sought from the ordinary courts. Investigative support is scoped to each tribunal's rules and confidentiality requirements.

How do you identify who controls a Prague holding company?

We start with the Czech commercial register, its collection of deeds and annual reports, then follow shareholdings into foreign registries where the structure leaves the Czech Republic. We add court records, regulatory decisions and Czech-language media. Where ownership remains unclear, we say so and set out what further lawful steps could resolve it.

Can TDSC conduct surveillance in Prague?

Not directly. Private detective services in the Czech Republic require a trade concession, which TDSC does not hold. Where surveillance or field enquiries are justified and lawful, we coordinate Czech professionals holding the concession and plan the work with local counsel, with attention to data protection and the proportionality of any observation.

What risks arise in Prague public procurement?

The main risks are undisclosed beneficial owners among bidders, conflicts of interest involving officials, and subcontracting chains that obscure who benefits from public or EU-funded contracts. We research ownership, prior procurement history, enforcement actions and political connections so that clients can make informed decisions about bids, partners and lending.
